questions.q: Fix: 'The concert was cancelled, many fans were disappointed.'
questions.a: Comma splice — fix as 'cancelled; many fans' or 'cancelled, so many fans' or a full stop. A wrong answer keeping the comma shows comma-power belief.

questions.q: Semicolon or comma: 'The exam was hard ___ it was fair.'
questions.a: Semicolon — two independent clauses, closely related, no conjunction. A wrong answer choosing comma creates a splice; 'and' + comma is the other legal fix.

questions.q: 'The students book's were stolen' — find both errors.
questions.a: 'students'' (possessive apostrophe after s) and 'books' (plural takes no apostrophe). A wrong answer fixing only one shows partial apostrophe rules.

questions.q: Punctuation is traffic control: commas separate but never join clauses; semicolons join related independent clauses without a conjunction; colons introduce lists/______; apostrophes mark possession and contraction — never plurals.

Fill in the blank: Punctuation is traffic control: commas separate but never join clauses; semicolons join related independent clauses without a conjunction; colons introduce lists/______; apostrophes mark possession and contraction — never plurals.
Fill in the blank: The comma's limits: 'It rained, we stayed home' is a splice — the comma cannot do a ______'s job.
What is Punctuation? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Punctuation is traffic control: commas separate but never join clauses; semicolons join related independent clauses without a conjunction; colons introduce lists/explanations; apostrophes mark possession and contraction — never plurals.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Punctuation?
questions.a: Students sprinkle commas as pauses ('wherever a breath fits'), use semicolons as super-commas, and apostrophize plurals ('apple's for sale').

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student punctuates complex sentences correctly — comma splices fixed, semicolons for balanced clauses, colons before lists, apostrophes confined to possession/contraction.
